questions.prompt: A request arrives as `POST /upload HTTP/1.1` with both `Content-Length: 10` and `Transfer-Encoding: chunked`. What does RFC 9112 allow an HTTP/1.1 server to do?
choices: Reject it with 400, or process it by `Transfer-Encoding` alone, and in both cases close the connection after answering
Use `Transfer-Encoding`, ignore `Content-Length`, and keep the connection open as usual
Use `Content-Length`, because it is the simpler framing
Read until the client closes the connection
questions.explanation: Two framing headers mean two possible readings of the same bytes, the shape of request smuggling. The RFC lets a server reject the request or trust Transfer-Encoding only, and requires it to close the connection afterwards so nothing after the ambiguous body is ever parsed as a request. minihttp and current nginx both answer 400 and close.

questions.prompt: A service sets a 30-second socket timeout before every `recv`. An attacker opens 500 connections and sends one header byte every 10 seconds on each. Which change stops the attack?
choices: Lower the per-read timeout to 15 seconds
Enable TCP keepalive probes every 10 seconds
A deadline for the whole header section counted from the connection's start or the request's first byte (nginx `client_header_timeout`), plus a limit on connections
Answer 408 as soon as the request line has arrived
questions.explanation: Every byte resets a per-read timeout, so any interval shorter than the timeout keeps the connection alive forever; 15 seconds still loses to one byte every 10. A total deadline does not reset. TCP keepalive only checks that the peer exists, which it does. minihttp's `read_head()` gets `deadline - now` for each read, and the slow-header test shows the cut at the deadline while drips keep arriving.

questions.prompt: nginx logs `upstream timed out (110: Connection timed out) while reading response header from upstream`. Which status did the client get, and which directive set the limit?
choices: 502, set by `proxy_connect_timeout`
504, set by `proxy_read_timeout`: the upstream sent nothing for that long between two reads
408, set by `client_body_timeout`
503, set by `keepalive_timeout`
questions.explanation: A timeout while waiting for the upstream is 504 Gateway Timeout. `proxy_read_timeout` applies between two successive reads, not to the whole response, so a slow upstream that trickles bytes can take longer in total. 502 is for refused, reset or malformed upstream responses, such as `connect() failed (111: Connection refused)`.

questions.prompt: A client sends `Connection: keep-alive, X-Trace` and `X-Trace: 1` through a reverse proxy. Following RFC 9110, which of these fields reach the upstream?
choices: Only `Connection`, because `X-Trace` is not a standard field
Both, unchanged
Only `X-Trace`; `Connection` is replaced
Neither: the proxy removes `Connection` and every field it names, then writes its own connection management
questions.explanation: Fields named in `Connection` are hop-by-hop by declaration, just like `Keep-Alive`, `TE` and `Transfer-Encoding`. minihttp's `forward_headers()` drops them. nginx removes its fixed list (`Connection`, `Keep-Alive`, `TE`, `Upgrade`, `Expect`, framing headers) but forwards `X-Trace`, which the probe's forwarding case shows.

questions.prompt: After an nginx upgrade, about 0.3% of POSTs fail with 502 and `upstream prematurely closed connection`, and GETs never fail. The app server closes idle connections after 5 seconds; nginx keeps idle upstream connections for 60. What is the right fix?
choices: Make the app's idle timeout longer than nginx's upstream `keepalive_timeout`, or lower nginx's below the app's, so nginx never reuses a connection the app is closing
Raise `proxy_read_timeout` to 120 seconds
Turn off chunked transfer coding on the app server
Add `proxy_next_upstream non_idempotent` so failed POSTs are retried
questions.explanation: Current nginx releases pool upstream connections by default. When nginx writes onto a connection the app has just closed, it retries the request on a new connection only for idempotent methods, so GETs hide the race and POSTs surface it. The idle timeouts must be ordered: the side that reuses a connection must give up on it before the side that closes it. Retrying POSTs can apply a payment twice.

questions.prompt: A download client resumes with `Range: bytes=1000-` and `If-Range: "6957-3f"`, but the file has changed since and now has a different ETag. What does the server send?
choices: 416 Range Not Satisfiable
304 Not Modified
206 with bytes 1000 onward of the new file
200 with the whole current file, because the If-Range validator no longer matches
questions.explanation: If-Range means "send me the range only if the representation is still the one I have; otherwise send all of it". Without it, the client would glue bytes of the new file onto the start of the old one. minihttp's `choose_range()` compares the strong ETag (or the exact Last-Modified date) and drops the Range header when it differs.
